explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. God tells Ezekiel to write, "Belonging to Judah and to the Israelites associated with him." (Ezekiel 37:16). So the first stick has Judah's name on it, plus the Israelites with him. Ezekiel is basically running a tiny label shop.

Levi was one of the twelve tribes of Israel (Genesis 49:28), so I see why he came to mind. But God doesn't tell Ezekiel to write Levi on a stick. The words are "Belonging to Judah and to the Israelites associated with him." Levi just didn't get a label this time.

Reuben was Jacob's firstborn (Genesis 49:3), so he's a name with some weight. Still, he's not the one God says to write on this stick. Ezekiel is told to write, "Belonging to Judah and to the Israelites associated with him." (Ezekiel 37:16). Judah is the name on the first stick.

That's right. God says, "Then join them together into one stick, so that they become one in your hand." (Ezekiel 37:17). Ezekiel takes two sticks and then gets told to join them into one. I'd have been standing there asking where the tape was.

It's the other way around, friend. God doesn't tell Ezekiel to keep the sticks apart. He says, "Then join them together into one stick, so that they become one in your hand." (Ezekiel 37:17). Two sticks go in, one stick comes out.

Not quite, friend. Ezekiel doesn't get to wing it when the people ask. God tells him to say that "…this is what the Lord GOD says…" (Ezekiel 37:19). He isn't sharing his own ideas. He's passing along what God said, and nobody has to guess.

Yes, that's False. When the people ask, Ezekiel is told to tell them "…this is what the Lord GOD says…" (Ezekiel 37:19). The explanation comes from God, not from Ezekiel's own thinking. Honestly, that's a relief for anybody who has ever been put on the spot with a question.

That's it. God says, "I will make them into a single stick, and they will become one in My hand." (Ezekiel 37:19). Earlier the sticks were one in Ezekiel's hand, and here God says they become one in His. That's the whole point of the sticks, friend.

House is a nice word, but it isn't the one in the verse. God says the sticks "…will become one in My hand." (Ezekiel 37:19). The picture is something held, like a stick in a hand. There's no house in it, and no mortgage either.

Heart sounds right, doesn't it? But the verse says, "…they will become one in My hand." (Ezekiel 37:19). That fits the stick picture, because you hold a stick in your hand. Sparkle is shaped like a heart and she's one of my cookie cutter kids, so I have a soft spot for that word.

That's the one. God says, "I will take the Israelites out of the nations to which they have gone, and I will gather them from all around and bring them into their own land." (Ezekiel 37:21). He gathers them from every direction and brings them home. I think I'd have kissed the ground.
Egypt is a fair guess, friend, but it's not in this promise. God says He will take them out of the nations and "…bring them into their own land." (Ezekiel 37:21). So the promise is their own land.

Babylon isn't in this promise, friend. God says He'll take the Israelites out of the nations they've gone to and "…bring them into their own land." (Ezekiel 37:21). He gathers them toward their own land, not toward another city.
Right on. God says, "…one king will rule over all of them." (Ezekiel 37:22). One nation, one king. Two kingdoms used to mean two sets of everything, and that's a lot of paperwork.
Close, but not the word God uses. He says, "…one king will rule over all of them." (Ezekiel 37:22). The job is king, and the number is one. Nobody's handing out a gavel here.
I can see why a priest came to mind, but it's not in this verse. God says, "…one king will rule over all of them." (Ezekiel 37:22). The ruler He names is a king, and there's only one of him.

Not this time, friend. God says the opposite: "…they will no longer be two nations and will never again be divided into two kingdoms." (Ezekiel 37:22). The word is never. There's no "maybe someday" in it.

Yes, False. God says they "…will no longer be two nations and will never again be divided into two kingdoms." (Ezekiel 37:22). Never means never, friend. Once God makes them one nation, they stay one.

explanations.answer: They will be His people and He will be their God
explanations.explanation: That's it. After saying He will cleanse them, God says, "Then they will be My people, and I will be their God." (Ezekiel 37:23). It's the closest, warmest line in the whole passage. I'd put it on the front of a cookie box.

explanations.answer: They will rule over all the nations around them
explanations.explanation: That sounds big, but it's not what God says here. After He cleanses them, He says, "Then they will be My people, and I will be their God." (Ezekiel 37:23). The promise is about belonging to Him, not ruling over everybody else.

explanations.answer: They will never face another enemy again
explanations.explanation: That's a nice-sounding promise, but verse 23 doesn't say it. What comes next is, "Then they will be My people, and I will be their God." (Ezekiel 37:23). That line is about belonging to Him.

You got it, baker. God says, "My servant David will be king over them, and there will be one shepherd for all of them." (Ezekiel 37:24). David was Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3), and here God calls him His servant. That's a title worth having.

Solomon, David's son who became king (1 Kings 1:39), is a fair guess. But the name God gives here is David. He says, "My servant David will be king over them, and there will be one shepherd for all of them." (Ezekiel 37:24).

Saul was a king of Israel too (1 Samuel 11:15), so the guess makes sense. But God doesn't name him here. He says, "My servant David will be king over them, and there will be one shepherd for all of them." (Ezekiel 37:24). It's David, friend.

That's the one. God says, "…I will make a covenant of peace with them; it will be an everlasting covenant." (Ezekiel 37:26). A covenant of peace that lasts forever. I could use some of that in my kitchen on batch day.

Salt is a real covenant word in the Bible, because Numbers 18:19 mentions a covenant of salt. But that's not what Ezekiel hears here. God says, "…I will make a covenant of peace with them; it will be an everlasting covenant." (Ezekiel 37:26).

A covenant of priesthood does show up in Numbers 25:13, so that's a real covenant word in the Bible. But in this verse God says, "…I will make a covenant of peace with them; it will be an everlasting covenant." (Ezekiel 37:26). The word here is peace, friend.
Yes, the nations. God says, "Then the nations will know that I the LORD sanctify Israel…" (Ezekiel 37:28). The nations are the ones who will know. That's a lot of nations learning one thing.
Priests are a natural guess, friend. But God says, "Then the nations will know that I the LORD sanctify Israel…" (Ezekiel 37:28). The ones who will know are the nations.
I get why that came to mind, friend, but it's not who the verse names. God says, "Then the nations will know that I the LORD sanctify Israel…" (Ezekiel 37:28). The nations are the ones who will know.
